title: Prologue — The eagle answered
description: Opens the deck with the eagle story. Full-bleed eagle image, story in the deck's serif, closing line set apart. Same prologue appears in the Practitioner Operating Plan deck and at the top of Headwaters Books and the Practitioner's Guide V2 home pages — one moment, four pieces.

title: Cover
description: Title slide for the Deer Lake Community General Store operational plan, delivered by Headwaters and written for the contractor and the band council to read together. Carries the V3 tagline: we've always known how to fix it, now we can.

title: The problem and the opportunity
description: Why a community-owned store now: incumbent reality, leakage estimate, subsidy pass-through, and the community-owned alternative. Lands on the V3 framing — Headwaters is paid for the operating system, not for the groceries; the store's grocery margin stays with the community.

title: Why current stores fail — market structure & ownership
description: First failure-surface slide drawn from the shared @workspace/why-stores-fail catalog: who owns the store, who decides what's on the shelf, and where the federal subsidy actually goes. Per-slide Sources footer generated from sourcesFooterLine().

title: Why current stores fail — supply chain & operations
description: Second failure-surface slide: how freight, hours-of-service rules, and a southern operating playbook break a northern store. Two-column layout (supply chain / operations) with named modes from the shared catalog and a per-slide Sources footer.

title: Why current stores fail — producer & financing side
description: Third failure-surface slide (producer wholesale lockout, capital access gap, processing infrastructure gap) plus the working community-owned counter-examples (Arctic Co-ops, Mistissini Meechum) and a per-slide Sources footer.

title: Supply chain and distribution
description: Three-lane supply model — the family-run refrigerated route through Dryden that already moves food on this corridor every two weeks, the winter-road truck added for Dryden → Deer Lake, and air freight when the road is closed. Curated shelf mix from regional farms and big-brand distributors.

title: Who works the store
description: The band staffs and runs the store. Headwaters delivers the operating system. The store is designed to keep working when people don't show up — pods not roles, cross-trained as baseline, software covers the gaps, shifts as a market, calendar that bends around community life. Practitioner visits monthly; bookkeeping handled remotely; technical advisor on retainer.

title: The first morning
description: Day-1 till configuration, offline mode, subsidy pass-through automation, freight cost on the tag, and the manager screen — built by Headwaters as the same transparency stack the public price dashboard and household lookup are built on.

title: The numbers, the schedule, who runs it
description: Planning-grade financial sketch (grocery spend, sales target, margin, opening cost, grant sources), 6 to 9 month launch gantt, and how the work splits — the band staffs and runs the store, Headwaters delivers software / tech stack at markup / training, the family-run refrigerated route handles the freight. The Headwaters operating fee is named honestly as TBD, sized in follow-up planning.

title: What Headwaters delivers
description: Three product layers — software the band owns, tech stack at markup, training programs — and what stays with Deer Lake on handoff: public price dashboard, household price lookup, the operating playbook, year-end value-delivered audit with the forward-credit clause. Total bill named as TBD pending follow-up sizing.

title: First reserve, then the next
description: Deer Lake is the first reserve Headwaters delivers to. Software, training, and the transparency stack are designed to be reused; the practitioner is the cross-reserve discipline-keeper who travels reserve to reserve to install Codetry, paid premium day rates ($3,500 on-site / $1,800 remote / $30k/yr retainer) with travel pass-through. Deer Lake graduates are local stewards of their own store. Carries the V3 thesis pull-quote: northern reserves need infrastructure as materially good as anything in the south, built on the foundation that's actually there — not less, different.

title: Risks and the ask
description: The seven things most likely to go wrong with a northern store launch and how Headwaters handles each, including the V3-named risk that people don't always show up. Closing ask: an hour with the contractor, an honest opinion, and an introduction to the band council when the contractor is ready. Signed Headwaters; no free lunches, value out the other end, forward-credit clause in writing.

title: The whole plan on one page — for council
description: Closing one-screen recap built so a council member can read it in under a minute and walk into a meeting with it. Three columns: what the store is in plain words (community-owned, leakage of $1.6–$2.0M, 84¢-on-the-shelf, family-run cold truck, Headwaters takes no cut of groceries, Arctic Co-ops / Mistissini precedent); the numbers ($400–700k to open, $90k/mo recommended plan, ~$181k day-one gap money, 17–20 jobs); and who runs what plus the one-line ask (band runs the store, Headwaters delivers the operating system, one hour + honest opinion + introduction). Same action+result voice as the rest of the deck. Designed to be the page you tear off and carry into the council meeting.
